questions.title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
questions.question: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking and when do you use each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Pessimistic: acquire lock before reading, hold until transaction ends — prevents concurrent access
- Optimistic: no lock on read; check version/timestamp at write time, fail if changed
- Pessimistic best for: high contention, short transactions, critical data (bank transfers)
- Optimistic best for: low contention, reads >> writes, web apps where conflicts are rare
- JPA: pessimistic with @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE), optimistic with @Version field
- Optimistic failure throws OptimisticLockException → retry or inform user

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Pessimistic locking locks the data as soon as you read it and holds that lock until your transaction is done. No other transaction can modify that data in the meantime. This guarantees consistency but hurts throughput — transactions queue up waiting for locks, and long-held locks can cause timeouts or deadlocks.

Optimistic locking doesn't take a lock at read time at all. Instead, you track a version number on each row. When you write, you check that the version hasn't changed since you read it. If another transaction modified the row in the meantime, the version won't match and your write fails with a conflict error. You then decide to retry or inform the user.

The right choice depends on contention. If many transactions are competing to modify the same data, optimistic locking becomes inefficient because retries mount up. High-contention scenarios like inventory reservation or account transfers benefit from pessimistic locking to ensure correctness without retries. For typical web application use cases where conflicts are rare — most users edit their own data — optimistic locking gives better throughput and doesn't waste locks on reads that might never conflict.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Pessimistic locking locks the data as soon as you read it and holds that lock until your transaction is done.
speakable_v2.cap: For typical web application use cases where conflicts are rare — most users edit their own data — optimistic locking gives better throughput and doesn't waste locks on reads that might never conflict.

questions.title: Deadlocks — Causes and Prevention
questions.question: What causes database deadlocks and how do you prevent them in a Spring application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Deadlock: two transactions each waiting for a lock held by the other
- DB detects cycle and kills one transaction (the deadlock victim)
- Prevention: acquire locks in consistent order across all code paths
- Prevention: keep transactions short, release locks quickly
- Prevention: use SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for queue-like processing
- Spring: handle DeadlockLoserDataAccessException with retry logic
- PostgreSQL logs deadlocks — check pg_log for deadlock graphs

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A deadlock happens when transaction A holds a lock that transaction B needs, and transaction B holds a lock that transaction A needs — they're each waiting for the other to release. Neither can proceed, so the database detects this cycle and terminates one of them, the deadlock victim, forcing the application to retry.

The most reliable prevention is acquiring locks in a consistent order. If every code path in your application always locks accounts in ascending ID order, you can never get into a circular wait — transaction A will always get account 100 before account 200, and so will transaction B. The deadlock only happens when one path locks 100 then 200 and another path locks 200 then 100.

Another major contributor is long-running transactions. The longer a transaction holds locks, the higher the chance another transaction needs the same resources. Keep transactions as short as possible — do all your computation and validation before starting the transaction, then execute the database writes quickly and commit.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: A deadlock happens when transaction A holds a lock that transaction B needs, and transaction B holds a lock that transaction A needs — they're each waiting for the other to release.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Keep transactions as short as possible — do all your computation and validation before starting the transaction, then execute the database writes quickly and commit.

questions.title: Transaction Isolation Levels in Depth
questions.question: What are the four transaction isolation levels and what anomalies does each level prevent?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- 4 levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE
- Each prevents progressively more anomalies (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read)
- PostgreSQL default: READ COMMITTED; MySQL InnoDB default: REPEATABLE READ
- READ UNCOMMITTED rarely used — allows dirty reads of uncommitted data
- SERIALIZABLE: most correct, heaviest locking or SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PG)
- Spring: set via @Transactional(isolation = Isolation.X)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The four isolation levels represent a spectrum from maximum concurrency to maximum correctness. READ UNCOMMITTED is the loosest — you can read data that another transaction hasn't committed yet, a dirty read. This is almost never used in practice because it allows reading garbage data.

READ COMMITTED is the most common default. You never read uncommitted data, but if you read the same row twice in one transaction and another committed transaction changed it in between, you might see different values — a non-repeatable read.

REPEATABLE READ guarantees that within one transaction, every read of the same row returns the same result regardless of concurrent commits. But a query that scans a range might return different rows if another transaction inserted new matching rows in between — a phantom read. SERIALIZABLE eliminates all anomalies by making concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, at the cost of the most contention.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Anomaly Scenarios

**Dirty Read** (READ UNCOMMITTED allows):
```
Tx A: UPDATE salary SET salary = 200000 WHERE id = 1  (not committed)
Tx B: SELECT salary WHERE id = 1  → sees 200000 (dirty!)
Tx A: ROLLBACK
Tx B: used a value that never existed
```

**Non-Repeatable Read** (READ COMMITTED allows):
```
Tx A: SELECT salary WHERE id = 1  → 80000
  ... Tx B commits: UPDATE salary SET salary = 95000 WHERE id = 1
Tx A: SELECT salary WHERE id = 1  → 95000  ← different! same tx, same query
```

**Phantom Read** (REPEATABLE READ allows):
```
Tx A: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > 1000  → 42 rows
  ... Tx B inserts new order with amount = 5000 and commits
Tx A: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > 1000  → 43 rows  ← phantom row!
```

## Levels and Prevention Table

| Level | Dirty Read | Non-Repeatable | Phantom |
|-------|-----------|-----------------|--------|
| READ UNCOMMITTED | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| READ COMMITTED | Prevented | Possible | Possible |
| REPEATABLE READ | Prevented | Prevented | Possible |
| SERIALIZABLE | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented |

## Setting in Spring

```java
// Default (READ_COMMITTED in PostgreSQL)
@Transactional
public void normalOperation() { ... }

// Consistent snapshot for financial reports
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ)
public FinancialReport buildReport() { ... }

// Maximum correctness for critical inventory operations
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.SERIALIZABLE)
public void reserveSeats(Long eventId, int count) { ... }
// PostgreSQL uses SSI — Serializable Snapshot Isolation
// Detects conflicts without locking, rolls back one of the conflicting transactions
```

speakable_v2.hook: The four isolation levels represent a spectrum from maximum concurrency to maximum correctness.
speakable_v2.cap: SERIALIZABLE eliminates all anomalies by making concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, at the cost of the most contention.

questions.title: Savepoints and Nested Transactions
questions.question: What are savepoints in SQL and how do nested transactions work in Spring with @Transactional propagation?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Savepoint: named checkpoint within a transaction — can rollback to it without ending the transaction
- Useful for partial rollbacks: try something risky, rollback to savepoint if it fails, continue
- Spring @Transactional propagation controls nested transaction behavior
- REQUIRED (default): joins existing transaction or creates new one
- REQUIRES_NEW: always creates a brand new transaction (suspends outer)
- NESTED: uses savepoints internally — partial rollback possible, commits with outer
- NOT_SUPPORTED: suspends current transaction, runs without one

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A savepoint is a named marker inside an ongoing transaction. You can roll back to the savepoint without undoing everything done before it in the same transaction. This allows you to attempt risky operations — like calling an external system or inserting into a table that might violate a constraint — and if it fails, roll back just that part and continue the rest of the transaction.

In Spring, propagation settings on @Transactional control how methods interact with existing transactions. The default, REQUIRED, means the method joins whatever transaction is already running, or starts a new one if there isn't one. REQUIRES_NEW always starts a fresh independent transaction — the outer transaction is suspended while the inner one runs. This is useful when you need an inner operation to commit even if the outer transaction rolls back, like writing an audit log.

NESTED uses database savepoints under the hood. It can roll back just the inner method's work while the outer transaction continues. Unlike REQUIRES_NEW, it commits with the outer transaction, so if the outer rolls back, the nested work rolls back too.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: A savepoint is a named marker inside an ongoing transaction.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Unlike REQUIRES_NEW, it commits with the outer transaction, so if the outer rolls back, the nested work rolls back too.

questions.title: Database Connection Pooling
questions.question: What is connection pooling and how do you tune HikariCP in a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Connection pooling: reuses existing DB connections instead of creating a new one per request
- Creating a new connection is expensive — TCP handshake, auth, SSL setup (~50ms+)
- HikariCP: Spring Boot's default pool — extremely fast and well-tested
- Key settings: maximumPoolSize, minimumIdle, connectionTimeout, idleTimeout, maxLifetime
- Pool size: not always bigger is better — too many connections can overwhelm the DB
- Rule of thumb: pool size = (core count × 2) + effective spindle count (Hikari recommendation)
- Monitoring: pool metrics via Micrometer/Actuator

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Opening a database connection is expensive — there's a TCP handshake, authentication, and possibly TLS negotiation, which together can take 50 milliseconds or more. For a web application handling hundreds of requests per second, creating a new connection per request would add unacceptable latency and overwhelm the database server with concurrent connections.

A connection pool maintains a set of already-open connections that requests borrow and return. HikariCP, Spring Boot's default, is designed to be extremely fast at this borrow-and-return cycle — it's one of the fastest JVM connection pools available.

A common mistake is setting the pool size too high. More connections isn't always better. PostgreSQL has an overhead per connection — memory for the connection's state, locks, and buffers. Beyond a certain point, adding connections actually hurts throughput due to lock contention and context switching. The right pool size is typically two times the number of CPU cores on the database server, not the application server.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## HikariCP Configuration

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb
    username: app_user
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10         # max connections in pool
      minimum-idle: 5               # min connections kept open
      connection-timeout: 30000     # max wait to get connection (ms)
      idle-timeout: 600000          # close idle connections after 10 min
      max-lifetime: 1800000         # max connection lifetime 30 min
      keepalive-time: 30000         # send keepalive every 30s
      pool-name: HikariPool-App
      # Validate connection is alive before lending
      connection-test-query: SELECT 1
```

## Pool Size Formula (Hikari's Recommendation)

```
pool_size = (num_db_cpu_cores × 2) + num_disk_spindles

Example: 4-core DB server, SSD storage (1 spindle equivalent)
pool_size = (4 × 2) + 1 = 9 → round to 10
```

## Monitoring Pool Metrics

```yaml
# Enable Hikari metrics via Actuator + Micrometer
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, metrics
```

```java
// Key Micrometer metrics to watch
// hikaricp.connections.active    → currently borrowed connections
// hikaricp.connections.pending   → threads waiting for a connection
// hikaricp.connections.timeout   → connections that timed out waiting
// hikaricp.connections.acquire   → time to borrow a connection

// Alert when: pending > 0 consistently, or timeout > 0
// Solution: increase pool size or reduce transaction hold time
```

## Common Mistake — Long-Running Transactions Exhaust Pool

```java
// BAD: holds a DB connection for the entire duration of an HTTP call to another service
@Transactional
public void processOrder(Order order) {
    orderRepo.save(order);   // borrows connection
    httpClient.notifyShipping(order);  // 2-second HTTP call — still holding connection!
    inventoryRepo.decrement(order);    // connection held entire time
}

// BETTER: release connection before external call
@Transactional
public void saveOrder(Order order) {
    orderRepo.save(order);  // connection released at method end
}

public void processOrder(Order order) {
    saveOrder(order);              // commits and releases connection
    httpClient.notifyShipping(order);  // external call without holding DB connection
    decrementInventory(order);     // new connection for this short tx
}
```

speakable_v2.hook: Opening a database connection is expensive — there's a TCP handshake, authentication, and possibly TLS negotiation, which together can take 50 milliseconds or more.
speakable_v2.cap: The right pool size is typically two times the number of CPU cores on the database server, not the application server.

questions.title: Avoiding Long-Running Transactions
questions.question: Why are long-running transactions harmful and what patterns help you avoid them?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Long tx holds locks — other queries queue up waiting, causing latency spikes
- Long tx delays VACUUM — dead tuples cannot be cleaned while old tx is open
- Connection pool exhaustion — borrowed connection is stuck for the duration
- Pattern: compute/fetch outside transaction, only write inside short transaction
- Pattern: batch processing with separate transactions per batch
- Avoid external HTTP calls or user interactions inside a transaction
- @Transactional on service layer, not on entire controller flow

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Long-running transactions cause cascading problems. The most immediate is lock contention — any rows you've written or locked in the transaction are unavailable to other queries until you commit. In a busy system, a transaction open for five seconds can cause hundreds of other queries to queue up waiting, creating visible latency spikes for users.

The second problem is VACUUM interference. PostgreSQL's AUTOVACUUM cannot reclaim dead tuple space that might be visible to open transactions. A single very old open transaction blocks cleanup across the entire database, causing table and index bloat to grow unchecked.

The main rule for avoiding long transactions is: compute everything you need before you start the transaction, then open the transaction, do the writes as quickly as possible, and commit. Never make external HTTP calls, process files, or wait for user input while a transaction is open. Those operations can take seconds or minutes and your database connection and all the locks it holds are stuck for that entire time.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.cap: Those operations can take seconds or minutes and your database connection and all the locks it holds are stuck for that entire time.

questions.title: Spring @Transactional Best Practices
questions.question: What are common mistakes and best practices with Spring's @Transactional annotation?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- @Transactional only works on public methods (Spring AOP proxy limitation)
- Self-invocation bypasses proxy — calling @Transactional from within same class doesn't work
- Default rollback: unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException); checked exceptions do NOT rollback
- Use rollbackFor for checked exceptions that should trigger rollback
- readOnly=true: optimization hint — disables dirty checking, enables read replica routing
- Don't put @Transactional on @Repository — put it on @Service (service layer owns transaction boundaries)
- Lazy loading outside transaction → LazyInitializationException

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The biggest @Transactional pitfall is self-invocation. Spring implements @Transactional using a proxy that wraps your bean. When you call a @Transactional method from within the same class, you're calling the raw object directly — the proxy is bypassed entirely and no transaction is started. This is a silent bug that's easy to miss because the code runs without error, just without a transaction.

The second most common mistake is assuming that all exceptions trigger a rollback. By default, Spring only rolls back on unchecked exceptions — RuntimeException and its subclasses. If you throw a checked exception, the transaction commits even if you intended a rollback. You need rollbackFor = Exception.class or throw a RuntimeException to ensure rollback on checked exceptions.

For read-only operations, mark the method with @Transactional(readOnly = true). This tells Hibernate to skip dirty checking on all loaded entities — a meaningful performance saving in methods that load many objects. It also enables routing to read replicas if you have that set up.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.cap: It also enables routing to read replicas if you have that set up.
